sources.notes: One collector, many feeds. Each feed carries its own attribution text; an item is attributed to its own national authority, never to ThreatPulse. Feeds that answer a browser challenge instead of a feed are excluded rather than retried: three were removed on 1 Nov 2026 because they rejected every automated request, with a browser User-Agent as well as ThreatPulse's own, so the block was not user-agent filtering and no plain HTTP client can read them. Retrying a challenge page only adds noise to the run report and traffic to a service that has asked to be left alone.

sources.name: MISP Galaxy
sources.licence: MISP Galaxy cluster data — AGPL-3.0 project, reused with attribution
sources.attribution_text: Source: MISP Galaxy (MISP project).
sources.notes: INGESTED as a KNOWLEDGE BASE, not a feed: it carries no observations and publishes nothing. It supplies an ALIAS BRIDGE to ATT&CK identifiers, so a malware family named on a threat still resolves when a feed spells the name differently from ATT&CK. Three of the forty galaxy files are fetched - mitre-enterprise-attack-malware, -tool and -intrusion-set - because measurement showed those are the only ones carrying meta.external_id, and every identifier in them is already in the ATT&CK index. They therefore add aliases and never new identifiers: 121 names ATT&CK does not carry, such as 'havex' for S0093, 'black energy' for S0089, 'schtasks.exe' for S0111 and 'cobalt gypsy' for G0059. The ransomware galaxy (2,179 values) and threat-actor galaxy (1,114 values) carry ZERO external_id values and cannot bridge to ATT&CK at all, so their 3.4 MB is deliberately not fetched. The gain is modest and is reported as modest.

sources.name: Fortinet PSIRT Advisories
sources.licence: Fortinet product security advisories, published openly for the use of Fortinet customers and the wider community
sources.attribution_text: Source: Fortinet PSIRT, Fortinet.
sources.notes: INGESTED. A first-party vendor advisory feed: Fortinet states the affected products and versions, which a CVE record alone does not. Ingested through the generic RSS collector, so no collector was written for it. Verified reachable without a key: fortiguard.com/rss/ir.xml returns HTTP 200.

sources.name: WordPress Security Releases
sources.licence: WordPress security announcements, published openly
sources.attribution_text: Source: WordPress Security Releases, WordPress Foundation.
sources.notes: INGESTED. Note the nature of this feed: it announces WordPress core and plugin security releases rather than publishing CVE records, so it contributes narrative context and advisory evidence more often than it contributes a scored vulnerability. Ingested through the generic RSS collector. Verified reachable without a key: wordpress.org/news/category/security/feed/ returns HTTP 200.

sources.name: Microsoft Security Update Guide
sources.licence: Microsoft Security Update Guide data, published openly for Microsoft customers and the wider community
sources.attribution_text: Source: Microsoft Security Update Guide, Microsoft.
sources.notes: INGESTED. Microsoft's FIRST-PARTY assessment of its own products, which no other source provides: its severity rating, its CVSS base score, the affected-product list, and the fixed build numbers an operator actually needs. A dependent per-CVE source, so it answers about the CVEs the pipeline already tracks and stays bounded per run. Uses the Security Update Guide OData API rather than CVRF: CVRF is XML and per-release, and the October 2026 document alone is 46.7 MB, whereas one CVE lookup here is about 1.5 KB. Verified live: the cveNumber filter returns the affected-product rows, an unknown CVE returns a count of 0 (a clean, cacheable miss), and $select is rejected with HTTP 403 so the payload cannot be trimmed server-side.

sources.name: CIRCL MISP OSINT Feed
sources.licence: Community-contributed MISP event data, published by CIRCL as an open feed
sources.attribution_text: Source: CIRCL MISP OSINT feed.
sources.notes: INGESTED. A COMMUNITY feed: CIRCL publishes what its contributors share, so an event is evidence that someone reported a campaign, not a vendor assessment. It is ingested because it is the only source enabled today that cites ATT&CK technique identifiers, and without one the ATT&CK enrichment has nothing to resolve against. Its events carry tags of the form 'misp-galaxy:mitre-attack-pattern="Hooking - T1179"', giving both the technique name and its identifier. Measured live: 1,681 events in the manifest, 123 carry a technique tag, 297 distinct technique identifiers across them, and a minority of events carry a restrictive traffic-light marking - so the marking is read PER EVENT and the gate applied to each, never inherited from the source. The manifest carries tags but not attributes, so techniques cost one request while CVEs and indicators cost one per event; event fetches are bounded per run and remembered in a cache. The wording above deliberately names no traffic-light level: the attribution register is published, and a published document that spells a restrictive marking out is refused by the quality gate - which is how this note was corrected.

sources.name: CAPEC
sources.licence: CAPEC is published by MITRE for public use with attribution
sources.attribution_text: Source: CAPEC (MITRE).
sources.notes: INGESTED as a KNOWLEDGE BASE, not a feed: it publishes no observations. It supplies the CWE-to-technique route, the only published bridge from a weakness to an attack pattern: CWE -> CAPEC -> ATT&CK technique. Measured live: the catalogue holds 615 patterns, 450 of them carrying a CWE, which is 1,212 links across 336 distinct CWEs; the ATT&CK bundle references 32 CAPEC patterns covering 36 techniques; so 31 of 336 CWEs reach a technique. Against this pipeline's own output the route carries 328 threats and 721 routes, taking ATT&CK enrichment from 23 threats to 347. TWO HONEST CAVEATS. (1) All 36 techniques the route can reach are RETIRED by ATT&CK - they were revoked or merged after the CAPEC cross-reference was written - so every technique reached this way is published with retired true and a consumer can see it. (2) An earlier note in this repository claimed CAPEC's XML contains no ATT&CK identifiers at all. That was wrong: CAPEC carries 272 taxonomy mappings to ATT&CK, but they name only the taxonomy with no Entry_ID, so they identify no technique. The conclusion held; the wording did not, and the wording is what a reader would have trusted.

sources.name: Cisco Security Advisories
sources.licence: Cisco publishes its security advisories publicly for the use of its customers and the wider community
sources.attribution_text: Source: Cisco Security Advisories, Cisco.
sources.notes: INGESTED. Cisco's own advisory feed, carrying its severity rating, its fixed-software statement and the CVE list per advisory. Ordinary RSS, so it reuses the generic collector rather than getting one of its own. NOTE ON ENDPOINTS: the publicationService.x JSON API returns an empty body with a 200 status, which is indistinguishable from a working endpoint that has nothing to say, so it is not used; the psirtrss20 RSS feed was verified to return 148 KB with 50 items, 48 of which name a CVE.

sources.name: Ubuntu Security Notices
sources.licence: Canonical publishes its security notices publicly for the use of its users and the wider community
sources.attribution_text: Source: Ubuntu Security Notices, Canonical.
sources.notes: INGESTED. Canonical states which of its releases a CVE affects and which packages fix it, which no upstream CVE record says. One request per run: the notices list carries the CVEs each notice addresses, so no detail fetch is needed. Ubuntu offers no per-CVE lookup - /security/CVE-2021-44228.json returns 404 for a CVE that certainly exists - so the dependent lookup pattern Red Hat and MSRC use is not available here. Both facts were checked before the collector was written.

sources.name: Sigma
sources.licence: Sigma rules are published under the Detection Rule License (DRL) 1.1
sources.attribution_text: Source: Sigma (SigmaHQ).
sources.notes: INGESTED as a KNOWLEDGE BASE, not a feed: it publishes no observations. It supplies DETECTION COVERAGE for a technique, which is what turns the ATT&CK context into something a defender can act on: a technique named beside a threat says what an adversary does, and a rule beside that technique says whether anyone has written a detection for it. Measured before building: the archive is 9.1 MB and holds 3,161 rule files, 2,817 of them carrying an attack.t tag, covering 390 distinct techniques through 3,819 rule-to-technique mappings. Of the 174 techniques this pipeline publishes, 128 have a rule and 46 do not - the 46 are as useful as the 128, because they are the techniques nothing detects yet. NO YAML PARSER IS USED: only the tags list entries and the title, level and status scalars are read, all line-oriented, so a malformed rule can at worst not appear. The regression_data tree is excluded deliberately - it holds info.yml files that sit under a rules path and look like rules but are test metadata, and the first file this parser read was one of them.
